summary.text: A continental margin is the outer edge of a continent's crust, where it meets oceanic crust beneath coastal waters.
It is made of three parts, the continental shelf, slope and rise, and together margins cover about 28% of the ocean's area.
Active margins sit at plate boundaries with volcanoes and earthquakes, while passive margins lie away from boundaries and are much wider and less steep.

items.prompt: Rivers wear sand and clay off the land and carry it to the sea. Roughly how much of that sediment gets trapped close to the continents, on their margins?

options.label: About 2%
About 80%
About 10%
About 30%

items.explain: Most river sediment settles near where rivers meet the sea: about 80% of the stream load is trapped and spread across continental margins.

items.prompt: A research ship sails from a beach straight out to the deep, flat ocean floor. In what order does it pass over the parts of the seafloor below?

options.label: Shelf, then slope, then rise
Slope, then shelf, then rise
Rise, then slope, then shelf
Shelf, then rise, then slope

items.explain: The shallow shelf runs out from the shore to the shelf break, the slope begins there, and the rise at the slope's base is the outermost zone before the abyssal plain.

items.prompt: The west coasts of North and South America see frequent volcanoes and earthquakes. What about their continental margins explains this?

options.label: They face a mid-ocean ridge
They hold kilometres of piled sediment
They have wide, gently sloping shelves
They lie along tectonic plate boundaries

items.explain: These are active margins, which are tied to plate boundaries and are places of high tectonic activity, including volcanoes and earthquakes.

items.prompt: A geologist wants several kilometres of well-kept sediment layers to study how ocean basins first formed. Where is her best bet?

options.label: A convergent margin like western South America
A transform margin full of offshore faults
A passive margin like the US East Coast
The steep shelf beside a deep trench

items.explain: Passive margins often hold several kilometres of sediment useful for studying ocean-basin formation, while tectonic activity leaves these deposits poorly preserved on active margins.

items.prompt: Why did nations set up the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, with rules tied to the edge of the continental margin?

options.label: To limit damage from undersea earthquakes
To settle claims as drilling, mining and fishing grew
To protect ships sailing through storms
To map the ocean floor for scientists

items.explain: The rise of offshore drilling, mining and the limits of fisheries led to the convention, which uses the margin's edge as one test for countries' claims to underwater resources.

items.prompt: Imagine draining the sea and walking across a typical continental shelf toward its outer edge. What would the ground feel like?

options.label: Steep, like climbing a mountainside
Rugged, with deep cliffs every few metres
A steady staircase of terraces
Almost perfectly flat underfoot

items.explain: The shelf is generally flat, with a mean angle of only 0° 07′; the steep drop comes only at the shelf break.

beats.title: Where Continents Really End
beats.hook: The beach is not the edge of a continent: its crust keeps going under the water before it meets the ocean's crust.

beats.prompt: Put these parts of the seafloor in order, heading out from the coast.
beats.explain: The flat shelf ends at the shelf break, where the slope begins; at the slope's base the seafloor levels out into the rise, the outermost zone of the margin.

beats.prompt: Sort each into the type of margin it belongs to.

left.label: East Coast of the United States
Narrow, with steep descents into trenches

beats.explain: Active margins sit at plate boundaries, so they are narrow, steep and shaken by tectonic activity; passive margins lie away from boundaries, are wide and gentle, and collect thick sediment.

choices.label: Dissolved away in the seawater
choices.feedback: Sand and clay are solid particles; they settle out rather than dissolving.

choices.label: Spread evenly over the deep-ocean basins
choices.feedback: It sounds fair to spread it everywhere, but most of it settles close to the continent.

choices.label: Carried out to the mid-ocean ridges
choices.feedback: Ridges are far out in the ocean; most sediment never travels that far from the river mouth.

paragraphs.heading: Where land meets the deep sea
paragraphs.text: A continental margin is the outer rim of a continent's crust, the place where it butts up against oceanic crust beneath coastal seas. Geologists count it as one of three big zones of the seafloor, alongside the deep-ocean basins and the mid-ocean ridges. Margins take up roughly 28% of the ocean's area.

paragraphs.heading: The shelf
paragraphs.text: Every margin has three parts: the continental shelf, the continental slope and the continental rise. Nearest the shore is the shelf, a fairly shallow and generally flat stretch of seabed running out from the coast toward open ocean. Shelves are thought to make up 7% of the sea floor, and their width ranges from 0.03 to 1500 km. The shelf ends at the shelf break, where the seabed suddenly tilts far more steeply.

paragraphs.heading: Down the slope to the rise
paragraphs.text: Beyond the break lies the continental slope, which can stand 1–5 km above the deep-ocean floor. Submarine canyons often slice into it; they tend to be V-shaped, with nearly vertical walls, and they can carve all the way down to the abyssal plain. At the foot of the slope the angle drops sharply and the seabed begins to level out. That gentler zone is the continental rise, the outermost part of the margin.

paragraphs.heading: Active margins
paragraphs.text: Margins come in two kinds, active and passive. Active margins usually sit at plate boundaries and are busy places, with volcanoes and earthquakes. The west coasts of North and South America are examples, and such margins tend to be narrow out to the shelf break before plunging steeply into trenches. Most are convergent, where an oceanic plate meets a continental one and the denser oceanic crust sinks beneath the lighter continental crust.

paragraphs.heading: Transform and passive margins
paragraphs.text: A rarer active kind, the transform margin, forms where an oceanic plate and a continental plate slide past each other in opposite directions. Many faults offshore there build rugged relief of islands, shallow banks and deep basins, known as the continental borderland. Passive margins usually lie inside plates, far from their edges, with little tectonic activity, and they often face mid-ocean ridges. They are much wider and gentler than active margins, with low land running for miles back from the beach, long rivers, and piles of sediment building up on the shelf. The East Coast of the United States is one.

paragraphs.heading: Where river sediment ends up
paragraphs.text: As continental rock weathers and wears away, it breaks down mostly into sand and clay, and much of it washes into rivers that empty into the sea. Of all the sediment rivers carry, 80% gets trapped and spread across continental margins. Shelves also hold a lot of glacial and relict sediment, laid down when sea level was lower. Passive margins can store several kilometres of sediment, which helps scientists study how ocean basins first formed, while on active margins tectonic activity often destroys such deposits.

paragraphs.heading: Why the shelf is valuable
paragraphs.text: In money terms, no part of the ocean is worth more than the shelf. It is often also the most productive and most studied part of the margin, since its shallow water is easy to reach. The spread of offshore drilling and mining, and the limits of fisheries, led to a United Nations treaty on the law of the sea, known as UNCLOS. Under it, the edge of the margin is one test for how far a country's claim to undersea resources reaches. Those resources include fishing grounds, oil and gas, sand, gravel and some heavy minerals, and valuable metal ores are thought to occur along certain active margins.
